newsitem.title: USA: U.S MUNICIPAL FOCUS - prices rebound from selloff.
newsitem.headline: U.S MUNICIPAL FOCUS - prices rebound from selloff.

text.p: U.S. municipal bonds rose an 1/8 to a 1/4 of a point at midday Thursday, as shortcovering and a continued lack of supply helped prices rebound from lows hit on Thursday due to fears of a monetary tightening.
Traders said that activity was fairly brisk, with also bottom-fishers in evidence, but noted that the performance of new issues appeared to be a bit spotty.

There was speculation that some dealers might have a few more bonds sold by the Municipal Assistance Corporation for New York City than they would have liked, though the $465 million offering has yet to be freed for trade.
Still, the deal appeared a bit pricey when measured against at least one possible benchmark, a $259 million offering by the New York State Thruway.
Those bonds, which were priced on Thursday with a top yield of 5.58 percent in 2017, got the benefit of a much more stable market than Wednesday's, when the MAC bonds for New York City were sold.
The MAC bonds were repriced, with the yield in 2008 raised five basis points to 5.05 percent, but some traders felt they should have been granted a bigger step-up in yield.
"MAC looked a little high next to the Thruway. I don't understand their thinking, maybe they feel the market will be a little better," a trader said.
Another trader pointed to a sizable $89 million balance remaining in Maryland's $240 million offering of general obligation bonds, which carry a top yield of 4.90 percent in the year 2008.
"It's a strong credit (but)...maybe the yields are not there for the funds," another trader said.
New issues sold on Thursday included Nassau County, New York, sold $185 million of bonds with a net interest cost of 5.1988 percent, in a comptetitive offering won by Prudential.

And traders noted the rise in rates since Thursday, when Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan warned he was prepared to pre-emptively raise rates if necessary and cautioned that the stock markets might not be able to sustain their gains, has awakened a bit more interest from retail investors.

"It's good for us that the long bond (Treasury) has gotten to a 6.78-79 percent yield. It's made for a little bit of interest," a trader said. The absence of individual investors for most of the past six to 12 months has hurt municipal markets, which have been shunned for better-performing equities.

U.S. March Treasury bond futures traded on the Chicago Board of Trade rose four ticks to 111, a rise exceeded by March municipal bond futures, which climbed 11 ticks to 116-4/32. This left the MOB spread at plus 132 ticks.

Actively quoted bonds in the secondary market included Denver Colorado City and County Airport Revenues of November 2025, which have a 5-1/2 percent coupon, and were bid at 5.80 percent, NET, down two basis points.
Florida Ports Financing Community Revenues of June 2027, which pay a 5-3/8 percent coupon, were offered at 5.80 percent, NET, up two basis points.
